domain_description: Tools for the work of coordinating what is taught against what is required and what is assessed. Coverage audits, framework crosswalks, KUD (Know/Understand/Do) chart authoring, and developmental band translation. The evidence question for this domain is different from intervention domains: alignment doesn't teach students — it helps the school's teaching reach what it intends to teach. The evidence base is methodological (Webb's Depth of Knowledge, Porter's content-analysis indices, Wiggins & McTighe's backward design, Squires' alignment scholarship) rather than pooled-effect-size; the value of these tools lies in process discipline and audit transparency, not in a per-student Cohen's d.

skills.description: Take a curriculum framework and a statutory or accreditation requirement list; produce a coverage table, gap summary, and CSV showing which framework content covers each requirement and where gaps exist. The audit itself doesn't teach — it surfaces what is and isn't covered, so the school can decide what to add, drop, or sequence differently. The evidence behind doing this work lives in Opportunity-to-Learn research: Schmidt, Guo & Houang (2021) found in US PISA 2012 mathematics data that OTL's effect on achievement was approximately 4× the effect of socioeconomic status; the TIMSS curriculum analysis tradition (Schmidt & Houang and colleagues across multiple cycles) consistently finds positive associations between coverage and achievement; Squires (2012) reviewed alignment research and reported consistent benefits when written, taught, and tested curriculum align. None of this generates a Cohen's d for the audit itself — the audit is a tool, and the gain materialises only if the school acts on what it reveals.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: The audit is essentially structured comparison work — a curriculum coordinator (or AI-assisted skill) reads both the framework and the requirement list, walks through the framework topic-by-topic noting coverage of each requirement, and produces the gap summary. Time investment is concentrated rather than ongoing: roughly 4–12 hours per subject per year for a first audit, less for repeat cycles once the comparison structure exists. The downstream cost — actually remediating identified gaps — varies enormously and lives in curriculum-redesign work, not in the audit itself. The audit's value compounds: schools that run it annually catch standard drift and accreditation surprises before they become crises. Verification-status note: shipped unverified because no meta-analysis exists for the audit-as-practice; the supporting Opportunity-to-Learn literature is correlational (Schmidt, Guo & Houang 2021 in Journal of Curriculum Studies; the TIMSS curriculum analysis tradition; Squires 2012 Clearing House alignment-research review) and addresses why content coverage matters rather than what a specific audit procedure produces.

skills.description: Compare two or more band-tagged curriculum frameworks and produce a framework-neutral topic matrix showing coverage and gaps across all inputs, plus an optional reference-centric Professional Learning Community crosswalk document when a reference framework is supplied. Anchored on the methodological scholarship of curriculum alignment: Webb's Depth of Knowledge (1997, 2007) for cognitive-complexity coding, Porter's alignment index (2002) for the P in [0,1] agreement metric between any two coded curricula, Hess's Cognitive Rigor Matrix (2004–2012) for combining Bloom's revised taxonomy with Webb's DoK, and Anderson & Krathwohl (2001) for the cognitive-process dimensions. These methodological frameworks are how alignment gets measured; the crosswalk applies them. Verification status: shipped unverified because a crosswalk is a methodological tool, not an intervention — the upstream evidence (Schmidt, Guo & Houang 2021's OTL finding, the TIMSS curriculum-coverage tradition) addresses why alignment matters, not what a specific crosswalk procedure produces. Source-voice preservation is built into the methodology: the matrix records each framework's own labels rather than rewriting them.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: A crosswalk is more demanding than a coverage audit because both (or all) input frameworks need to be coded into the same content × cognitive matrix before they can be compared — and that coding is non-trivial when the source frameworks use different terminology, granularity, and implicit cognitive expectations. A two-framework crosswalk typically takes 12–25 hours per subject for a first pass; the time scales roughly linearly with the number of frameworks compared. Schools with internal curriculum coordinators already trained in Webb/Hess methodology absorb this cost more efficiently than schools commissioning external alignment consultants. The output's value compounds: once two frameworks are crosswalked, future additions (a new textbook, a new state standard, a new assessment) can be mapped against the same neutral matrix rather than re-comparing pairwise. Same unverified-because-methodological pattern as the Coverage Audit card.

skills.description: Author or review Know / Understand / Do (KUD) charts for competency-based learning targets across developmental bands. KUD is the operational tool from Wiggins & McTighe's Understanding by Design framework: distinguish the factual knowledge students should know, the enduring understandings they should grasp (transferable cross-context concepts), and the skills and performances they should be able to do. Handles seven input types from raw curriculum documents to existing learning-target sets; routes to upstream skills when stronger inputs are available. Verification status: shipped unverified. The UbD framework has substantial qualitative research — Yurtseven 2021 meta-synthesis found consistent positives for cognitive growth, engagement, and motivation but documented persistent implementation gaps where teachers stay anchored to activity-based rather than backward design. No quantitative meta-analysis with pooled Cohen's d exists. The discipline of the KUD chart is what it forces: identifying enduring understandings (Wiggins & McTighe 2005) rather than just topical content.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: The KUD chart itself is structurally simple — three columns, items per column — but writing a good one requires content expertise (especially for the Understand tier, where naming the durable transferable concept is non-trivial) and UbD training. Teachers without backward-design experience tend to overload the Know column with topics, leave the Understand column thin, and fill the Do column with classroom activities rather than performances of understanding. PD investment for a department to author quality KUD charts is roughly 8–16 hours of structured work plus ongoing peer review. The chart pays off across multiple downstream products: it constrains learning-target writing, anchors assessment design, and surfaces gaps between intended understanding and what classroom activities actually develop. Same unverified-because-methodological pattern as Coverage Audit and Curriculum Crosswalk — UbD is a framework with strong qualitative research (Yurtseven 2021 meta-synthesis) but no pooled student-outcome effect size.

skills.description: Tag harness-decomposed curriculum items (KUDs, learning targets, criteria) with a school's developmental-band metadata while preserving source voice and labels. Supply the band schema; the skill derives mapping rules from it rather than imposing external bands. The theoretical anchor is Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development — tasks within a learner's ZPD produce growth; tasks below produce coasting and tasks above produce stagnation. The methodological tradition is learning progressions (Heritage 2008, Corcoran, Mosher & Rogat 2009, Taking Science to School National Academies 2007) and Wiggins & McTighe's developmental considerations in Understanding by Design. Verification status: shipped unverified. No meta-analysis quantifies the effect of band-tagging itself; the gain materialises in classroom design downstream — teachers using the band-tagged map to sequence tasks at appropriate difficulty — and that design work is not separable from the broader pedagogical decisions the school makes around it. Source-voice preservation matters: the skill records each item under the school's own band labels rather than reanchoring to an external taxonomy, so the work survives schema migration and accreditation review.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: The tagging itself is operationally straightforward once the band schema is articulated — items get walked against the schema's descriptors and assigned. The substantive cost lives upstream and downstream: (1) upstream, the school needs a clear band schema with cognitive descriptors per band (often itself an effortful curriculum-team product, especially if the school has just adopted a new framework with different bands); (2) downstream, the band-tagged map only produces gains if teachers actually use it to sequence tasks at ZPD-aware difficulty. A naive band tag without instructional follow-through changes nothing in classrooms. Initial tagging is typically 6–15 hours per subject; ongoing maintenance is low once the schema stabilises. Same unverified-because-methodological pattern as the other three cards in this domain — Vygotsky's ZPD and the learning-progressions tradition are conceptually robust but the band-tagging procedure itself has no pooled student-outcome effect size.
